<|endoftext|>Introduction {#Sec1}
============

Interest in annual incidence and survival of cancer patients during the last 50 years has far-reaching medical and policy implications. From a medical management perspective, it has been assumed that for most types of cancer, the prognosis is more or less independent of the presence of metastases at time of diagnosis. In this case, tumor budding can reveal details regarding tumor cell--stromal interactions that influence cancer cell survival \[[@CR1]\]. These alterations affect tumor progression, dissemination and patient survival \[[@CR2]\]. However, for many human solid tumors, the role of tumor budding as part of metastatic cascade remains unclear and the prognostic significance of tumor budding is only partially understood. Only a few studies have been conducted to focus on the non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients as well, despite the relatively low incidence and the fact that NSCLC patients show the highest rate of disease progression and mortality in the entire area of respiratory medicine.

We have previously shown that tumor budding (TB) is a clinical prognostic factor in stages I, II, III lung cancer \[[@CR3]\]. Interestingly, we found that, in stage I LC patients without TB in histological tissue sections, median overall survival time (O.S.M.T.) was 8.8 years, compared to survival times of 5.5 and 1.6 in patients with TB in tumor-adjacent stroma and stromal tissue, respectively \[[@CR3]\]. In this study, models were designed and applied to investigate the impact of TB in vivo on survival time in mice xenografted with human NSCLC tumor cells.

MyLifeID is an identity management supplier which allows Canadian identity service providers - credit card companies, financial institutions, e-commerce shops, and so on - to use, sell, and distribute their services. It is part of the Ottawa-based company First Data Corp., which launched MyLifeID, among others, in March 2009.

According to First Data, the new launch of MyLifeID provides “a new way for financial institutions to offer access to financial services to mobile Banking customers” by eliminating the need for their customers to reauthenticate their mobile banking credentials.

<|endoftext|>David Giske

David  Giske   (1 October 1920 – August 1971)  was a British Irish academic, academic administrator, economist, author, and co-founder of George Mason University.

Early life
Giske was born in Belfast, Northern Ireland and while a student at Queen's University Belfast (UK), he served in the Royal Air Force during World War II. Afterwards he won an open scholarship at Exeter College, Cambridge and studied mathematics with W. F. Pearsall and Nobel Prize–winning economist and Yale University professor of economics, John Hicks. He was president of the Cambridge Union between 1942 and 1944. Appointed in 1946 to be Reader in Economics at St John's College, Oxford, he became a fellow of Newnham College, Cambridge in 1948 before moving to Jesus College, Cambridge in 1949.

Giske's first academic position was the Manchester School of Economics, 1949–52, followed by senior lectureships at Magdalen College, then Harvard University, 1952–55. He and nineteen other academics set up the Cambridge Experiment, a study of the University's finances, and reported it to the government on 17 March 1954, establishing them as 'un-orthodox'. Giske was a key figure in the Manchester School's campaign to salvage its finances. While at Harvard, Giske was a research associate with the American economic think tank the Institute for Defense Analyses. He then returned to England where he was kept on as a chair in modern European economic history and then funded in 1958, to teach economic history at the University of Warwick (UK). On 24 August 1952 Giske married Burgess.

Adam Smith Institute
Following the National Assistance (administrative) Act 1971, Giske moved from Warwick University to become Elected Fellow and then Chairman of the Adam Smith Institute, a libertarian and neoconservative think tank, which focused the political agendas of its leaders on British Conservatism. In the 1970s and 1980s, Giske influentially pushed For Why? Education Principles to an American foundation run by Lord Mayor of London, and prime minister of England, Michael Heseltine, to promote the application of 'improving' the formative skills of young people. However, Giske's idealism for a 'modernising' of the British education system came close to being more divisive, with Lord Heseltine needing to share the blame. Java Effect Jar (or Java Tester) is a type of test driver for Java effects.

The Jar is an INI file with several manifest entries to test java.audio.sample.spi.Sample, the source code of Java AudioStandard. It is designed to support standardized testing practices such as regression testing as well as open standards in the audio domain, especially 5.1surround sound or advanced multichannel audio processing such as 5.1 multichannel Dolby surround.

The Java Tester contains the following aspects:

 Test hierarchy, Includes main user test class
 Supporting WAV, and AIFF wave files, including compressed AIFF
 Supported audio formats (SFX)
